notes: Selenographic coordinates in degrees, planetocentric (Mean Earth/Polar Axis), east longitude positive (-180..180), south negative. Historic coordinates: LROC/Wagner et al. 2017 (Icarus 283) where available, NASA/LROC/peer-reviewed papers for recent landers, NSSDC nominal values for Luna 9 and 13 (not confirmed in LRO images). Artemis candidate region centres: centre of the lon/lat bounding box of each region's 1 km navigation grid in the USGS ScienceBase release (regions sourced from LROC QuickMap); Mons Mouton Plateau uses the centre of LROC's plateau NAC mosaic because its USGS file is not downloadable. These are region centres, not landing points. Region centres for other planned missions use the IAU Gazetteer centre of the named feature (crater, swirl, plateau). Several south-pole pins sit near Mons Mouton (IM-2, IM-4, Griffin-1, Chang'e-8, two Artemis regions): cluster or offset labels in the UI. Status as of 2026-11-16: no lunar landings in 2026 so far. Artemis II flew Apr 2026; Artemis III (2027) is an Earth-orbit docking test; Artemis IV (early 2028) is the first crewed landing. Chang'e-7 missed its Aug 2026 window (now reported 2027). Skipped for lack of a current published site: LUPEX/Chandrayaan-5 (site not fixed), ILRS base (only 'south pole region'), ispace Mission 3 ULTRA (site not published), Draper/ispace CP-12 Schrödinger mission (cancelled July 2026). label: Fact = primary source for site and status; Reported = secondary source, announced-but-unconfirmed, or conflicting sources (see each record's note).

sites.name: Peak near Cabeus B
sites.status: candidate region; first landing planned early 2028
sites.why_here: A tall peak next to Cabeus crater gets long hours of sunlight while nearby crater floors stay in deep shadow, where ice may hide.
sites.fun_fact: In 2009 NASA's LCROSS probe crashed into Cabeus crater on purpose and found water in the dust it kicked up.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: One of NASA's 9 candidate regions (announced Oct 2024 for Artemis III; landing moved to Artemis IV in 2026). Coordinate = centre of the region's USGS/LROC grid bounding box; each region holds several possible sites.

sites.name: Haworth
sites.status: candidate region; first landing planned early 2028
sites.why_here: Haworth crater's floor never sees the Sun, so it is a natural freezer that may hold ice; astronauts could land on sunny ground at its edge.
sites.fun_fact: The bottom of a crater like Haworth can be colder than -200 °C, colder than anywhere on Earth.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: One of NASA's 9 candidate regions (announced Oct 2024 for Artemis III; landing moved to Artemis IV in 2026). Coordinate = centre of the region's USGS/LROC grid bounding box; each region holds several possible sites.

sites.name: Malapert Massif
sites.status: candidate region; first landing planned early 2028
sites.why_here: Malapert is a big mountain block that can often see Earth, which helps radio contact, and has gentle slopes in places.
sites.fun_fact: From high on Malapert, Earth hangs low over the horizon and barely moves in the sky.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: One of NASA's 9 candidate regions (announced Oct 2024 for Artemis III; landing moved to Artemis IV in 2026). Coordinate = centre of the region's USGS/LROC grid bounding box; each region holds several possible sites.

sites.name: Mons Mouton Plateau
sites.status: candidate region; first landing planned early 2028
sites.why_here: The flat top of Mons Mouton is high enough to catch a lot of sunlight and wide enough for a safe landing and long drives.
sites.fun_fact: Mons Mouton is named after Melba Roy Mouton, a NASA mathematician who tracked satellites in the 1960s.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: One of NASA's 9 candidate regions (announced Oct 2024 for Artemis III; landing moved to Artemis IV in 2026). Coordinate = centre of LROC's Mons Mouton Plateau NAC mosaic (USGS grid file not downloadable); each region holds several possible sites.

sites.name: Mons Mouton
sites.status: candidate region; first landing planned early 2028
sites.why_here: The slopes of Mons Mouton lie close to cold, shadowed spots, so astronauts could land in sunlight and walk toward possible ice.
sites.fun_fact: Mons Mouton is about 6 km tall, taller than any mountain in North America measured from its base.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: One of NASA's 9 candidate regions (announced Oct 2024 for Artemis III; landing moved to Artemis IV in 2026). Coordinate = centre of the region's USGS/LROC grid bounding box; each region holds several possible sites.

sites.name: Nobile Rim 1
sites.status: candidate region; first landing planned early 2028
sites.why_here: This spot on the rim of Nobile crater sits beside shadowed ground that may trap ice, with sunny areas for landing.
sites.fun_fact: Nobile crater is named after Umberto Nobile, an Italian explorer who flew an airship over the North Pole on Earth.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: One of NASA's 9 candidate regions (announced Oct 2024 for Artemis III; landing moved to Artemis IV in 2026). Coordinate = centre of the region's USGS/LROC grid bounding box; each region holds several possible sites.

sites.name: Nobile Rim 2
sites.status: candidate region; first landing planned early 2028
sites.why_here: Another part of Nobile crater's rim offers very old rocks and nearby icy shadows to study.
sites.fun_fact: Nobile crater is about 79 km across, wider than the city of London.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: One of NASA's 9 candidate regions (announced Oct 2024 for Artemis III; landing moved to Artemis IV in 2026). Coordinate = centre of the region's USGS/LROC grid bounding box; each region holds several possible sites.

sites.name: de Gerlache Rim 2
sites.status: candidate region; first landing planned early 2028
sites.why_here: This region is one of the closest to the south pole, on the rim of de Gerlache crater, with long sunlight and deep cold traps nearby.
sites.fun_fact: De Gerlache crater is named after a Belgian who led one of the first expeditions to spend a winter in Antarctica.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: One of NASA's 9 candidate regions (announced Oct 2024 for Artemis III; landing moved to Artemis IV in 2026). Coordinate = centre of the region's USGS/LROC grid bounding box; each region holds several possible sites.

sites.name: Slater Plain
sites.status: candidate region; first landing planned early 2028
sites.why_here: A fairly flat plain near the pole, which makes landing safer, with shadowed craters close enough to explore.
sites.fun_fact: Near the lunar south pole the Sun always stays low, so shadows of rocks can stretch for very long distances.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: One of NASA's 9 candidate regions (announced Oct 2024 for Artemis III; landing moved to Artemis IV in 2026). Coordinate = centre of the region's USGS/LROC grid bounding box; each region holds several possible sites.

sites.name: Shackleton crater rim
sites.why_here: The rim of Shackleton crater is sunny for most of the year, while the crater floor next to it is always dark and may hold ice. A small hopping robot will jump into the shadow to look for water.
sites.fun_fact: Chang'e-7 carries a flying 'hopper' that leaps around using small rocket engines instead of wheels.
sites.label: Reported
sites.note: Target 'illuminated rim of Shackleton' is official (CE-7 team, National Science Review 2024). The 88.8S 123.4E point is from a 2023 Chinese social-media post cited by Wikipedia; treat as approximate. Launch window in Aug 2026 was abandoned (CMSA statement via Ars Technica, 23 Aug 2026); 2027 is reported, no official new date.

sites.name: Leibnitz-Beta Plateau (Mons Mouton)
sites.why_here: China picked this high plateau near the south pole to test making bricks and using local materials, early steps toward a research base.
sites.fun_fact: Chang'e-8 plans to test 3D-printing building blocks from Moon soil.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: CNSA (Xinhua via gov.cn, 24 Apr 2025): target is the Leibnitz-Beta Plateau. Coordinate is the IAU centre of Mons Mouton (formerly Leibnitz Beta).

sites.name: Rimae Bode (proposed)
sites.status: proposed by scientists; crewed landing planned by 2030
sites.why_here: Scientists suggested this flat area near the Moon's equator because it is safe to land on, always faces Earth for easy radio contact, and has volcanic glass beads to sample.
sites.fun_fact: Tiny glass beads here formed in lava fountains billions of years ago.
sites.label: Reported
sites.note: Not an official choice: a 2026 study (reported by Scientific American, 10 Mar 2026) names Rimae Bode as a high-priority site. China has not published its crewed landing site. Coordinate = IAU centre of Rimae Bode.

sites.name: Reiner Gamma
sites.why_here: Reiner Gamma is a bright swirl pattern linked to a patch of magnetism in the Moon's crust. Scientists want to learn why the swirl stays bright.
sites.fun_fact: From Earth with a telescope, Reiner Gamma looks like a pale tadpole painted on a dark sea.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: Site Reiner Gamma is from NASA. Launch NET Q1 2027 is from Wikipedia/press (Reported). Coordinate = IAU centre of Reiner Gamma.

sites.name: Mons Mouton
sites.why_here: IM-4 carries a European drill to look for water ice in the ground near Mons Mouton, close to where Athena landed in 2025.
sites.fun_fact: The drill is built by the European Space Agency to dig into the soil and sniff for water.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: Coordinate = IAU centre of Mons Mouton; exact landing point not published.

sites.name: Near Mons Mouton (Griffin-1)
sites.why_here: Griffin-1 will carry the FLIP rover to test driving on rough polar ground, the kind of trip future astronaut rovers will make.
sites.fun_fact: Griffin-1 will carry more than 450 kg of cargo, the largest commercial load ever sent to the Moon's surface.
sites.label: Reported
sites.note: Sources disagree: NASA's event page says Nobile crater; Voyager (22 Oct 2026) says 'near Mons Mouton'. Pin uses the newer company statement at the IAU Mons Mouton centre. Launch: NASA said late 2026 (Aug 2026); later reports say NET Jan 2027.

sites.name: Shackleton Connecting Ridge
sites.mission: Blue Moon MK1 'Endurance' pathfinder (NASA Moon Base I)
sites.why_here: This ridge between Shackleton and de Gerlache craters is sunlit most of the time, so a lander can get solar power for long periods. The test helps prepare crewed landings.
sites.fun_fact: The lander is named Endurance after Ernest Shackleton's ship that sailed toward Earth's South Pole.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: Site name from NASA. Coordinate is the well-studied 'connecting ridge' site 001 (89.45S, 222.69E) from illumination papers, not a Blue Origin-published point.

sites.name: Nassau crater (far side)
sites.why_here: The far side is shielded from Earth's radio noise, so a radio telescope here (LuSEE-Night) can listen for faint signals from the early universe.
sites.fun_fact: It would be the first American landing on the far side of the Moon.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: Firefly names Nassau crater as the landing site. Coordinate = IAU centre of Nassau.

sites.name: Gruithuisen Domes
sites.why_here: These rounded hills look like volcanoes made of sticky, silica-rich lava, which is rare on the Moon. A rover will help work out how they formed.
sites.fun_fact: On Earth, domes like these usually need water to form, which makes the Moon's version a puzzle.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: Coordinate = IAU centre of Mons Gruithuisen Gamma (one of the domes).

sites.name: Haworth crater
sites.why_here: Two rovers will explore near Haworth crater, whose dark floor may hold ice, to help plan the Moon Base.
sites.fun_fact: Haworth is also one of NASA's candidate regions for astronauts.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: Firefly: 'Moon's South Pole, Haworth Crater'. Coordinate = IAU centre of Haworth; the lander will be on the rim, exact point not published.

sites.name: Near Shiv Shakti point
sites.why_here: ISRO plans to land close to where Chandrayaan-3 landed, an area it already knows well, and bring Moon soil back to Earth.
sites.fun_fact: It would be India's first mission to bring Moon samples home.
sites.label: Reported
sites.note: Site 'near Shiv Shakti' is from a 2024 talk by the SAC director reported by India Today; no official coordinates. Pin shares Chandrayaan-3's point. 2028 date from press/Wikipedia.

sites.name: Tranquility Base
sites.why_here: The Sea of Tranquility is a smooth, flat lava plain near the Moon's equator, which made it a safe choice for the very first human landing.
sites.fun_fact: Neil Armstrong had to steer past a field of boulders and landed with less than a minute of descent fuel left.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Ocean of Storms (Surveyor 3 site)
sites.why_here: NASA wanted to prove astronauts could land exactly on target, so they aimed right next to the robot lander Surveyor 3.
sites.fun_fact: The astronauts walked over to Surveyor 3 and brought pieces of it back to Earth.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Fra Mauro
sites.why_here: The Fra Mauro hills are made of rock thrown out by the giant impact that formed Mare Imbrium, so they could reveal the Moon's early history.
sites.fun_fact: Alan Shepard hit two golf balls on the Moon.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Hadley-Apennine
sites.why_here: This spot has tall mountains and a winding valley called Hadley Rille, giving astronauts many kinds of rock to sample.
sites.fun_fact: Apollo 15 was the first mission to drive a car on the Moon, the Lunar Roving Vehicle.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Descartes Highlands
sites.why_here: Apollo 16 was the only mission to land in the bright highlands, the oldest crust on the Moon's near side.
sites.fun_fact: Charlie Duke left a family photo on the Moon; it is still there.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Taurus-Littrow
sites.why_here: This valley has both old highland rock and younger volcanic material, and the crew included the first geologist on the Moon.
sites.fun_fact: Apollo 17 is the most recent time people walked on the Moon.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Oceanus Procellarum (Luna 9)
sites.why_here: Engineers needed a flat lava plain to try the first soft landing; the Ocean of Storms was a good, broad target.
sites.fun_fact: Luna 9 sent back the first pictures ever taken from the surface of another world.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: Lander not yet confirmed in LRO images; nominal mission coordinates.

sites.name: Oceanus Procellarum (Luna 13)
sites.why_here: Another flat lava plain, chosen so the lander could test how firm the Moon's soil is.
sites.fun_fact: Luna 13 poked the ground with a spring-loaded arm to check if the soil could hold up a spacecraft.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: Nominal mission coordinates.

sites.name: Mare Fecunditatis (Luna 16)
sites.why_here: A smooth lava sea near the equator was easy to reach and safe for the first robot that scooped soil and flew it back to Earth.
sites.fun_fact: Luna 16 brought home 101 grams of Moon soil, about the weight of an apple.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Mare Imbrium (Lunokhod 1)
sites.why_here: The wide, flat Sea of Rains was a good place for the first remote-controlled rover to drive.
sites.fun_fact: Lunokhod 1 was driven by a team on Earth and travelled about 10 km.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Apollonius highlands (Luna 20)
sites.why_here: Luna 20 landed in hilly highlands next to Mare Fecunditatis to bring back older, lighter-coloured rock.
sites.fun_fact: Luna 20 landed only about 130 km from where Luna 16 had landed.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Le Monnier crater (Lunokhod 2)
sites.why_here: Le Monnier is an old flooded crater at the edge of Mare Serenitatis where lava plains meet mountains, an interesting place to drive a rover.
sites.fun_fact: Lunokhod 2 drove about 39 km, a distance record that stood for decades.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Mare Crisium (Luna 24)
sites.why_here: Mare Crisium is a round lava sea; Luna 24 drilled about 2 metres down to collect a long core of layered soil.
sites.fun_fact: Luna 24 was the last Moon landing for 37 years, until Chang'e 3 in 2013.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Flamsteed P (Surveyor 1)
sites.why_here: NASA chose a flat lava plain in the Ocean of Storms to test whether a robot could land softly before sending astronauts.
sites.fun_fact: Surveyor 1 was the first American spacecraft to land softly on the Moon and took over 11,000 pictures.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Guang Han Gong (Mare Imbrium)
sites.why_here: A flat part of Mare Imbrium gave China a safe first landing for its lander and Yutu rover.
sites.fun_fact: Yutu means 'Jade Rabbit', the pet rabbit of the Moon goddess Chang'e in Chinese legend.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Statio Tianhe (Von Kármán crater)
sites.why_here: Von Kármán crater sits inside the Moon's biggest, oldest impact basin, so rocks from deep inside the Moon may be found there.
sites.fun_fact: Chang'e 4 made the first ever landing on the far side of the Moon, talking to Earth through a relay satellite.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Statio Tianchuan (near Mons Rümker)
sites.why_here: The lava here is much younger than at the Apollo sites, so its samples help scientists date the Moon's volcanic history.
sites.fun_fact: Chang'e 5 brought home 1,731 grams of Moon rock and soil.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Apollo basin (far side)
sites.why_here: The Apollo basin lies inside the giant South Pole-Aitken basin; samples from here tell us about the far side, which no one had sampled before.
sites.fun_fact: Chang'e 6 brought back the first ever samples from the far side of the Moon.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Shiv Shakti point
sites.why_here: India aimed for high southern latitudes, closer to the icy south pole than anyone had landed before, on fairly flat ground.
sites.fun_fact: India became the fourth country to land softly on the Moon; 23 August is now its National Space Day.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: Region tag 'south-pole' follows ISRO's description; at 69.4S it is a high southern latitude rather than the polar cap.

sites.name: Shioli crater (Mare Nectaris)
sites.why_here: JAXA picked a spot beside a small crater to prove its lander could touch down within about 100 metres of its target.
sites.fun_fact: SLIM landed upside down on its nose but still worked and took pictures.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Malapert A (Odysseus)
sites.why_here: Odysseus went far south, near Malapert A crater, to test landing in the rough terrain close to the south pole.
sites.fun_fact: Odysseus tipped over onto its side but still sent data, and was the first US Moon landing since 1972.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Mons Latreille (Mare Crisium)
sites.why_here: Mare Crisium is a flat lava basin next to an old volcanic peak, Mons Latreille; it was safe to land and good for studying heat flow and dust.
sites.fun_fact: Blue Ghost was the first commercial lander to land upright and complete its whole mission.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Mons Mouton plateau (Athena)
sites.why_here: Athena aimed for the high plateau of Mons Mouton to drill for ice and test a hopping drone close to the south pole.
sites.fun_fact: Athena landed farther south than any spacecraft before it, but ended up on its side inside a small crater.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Beresheet crash site
sites.why_here: Beresheet was aiming for the flat Sea of Serenity when an engine problem caused it to crash.
sites.fun_fact: Beresheet was the first privately funded attempt to land on the Moon.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: Vikram (Chandrayaan-2) crash site
sites.why_here: Vikram was trying to land on high southern plains between two craters when it lost control just above the surface.
sites.fun_fact: NASA's orbiter found the debris with help from a volunteer, Shanmuga Subramanian, who spotted it in the photos.
sites.label: Fact
sites.note: Crash time was 6 Sep 2019 ~20:23 UTC (7 Sep in India).

sites.name: Luna 25 crash site
sites.why_here: Luna 25 was heading for a south polar site when a faulty engine burn sent it into the Moon instead.
sites.fun_fact: NASA's orbiter spotted a new 10-metre crater that was most likely made by Luna 25.
sites.label: Fact

sites.name: RESILIENCE crash site (Mare Frigoris)
sites.why_here: ispace aimed for the flat lava of Mare Frigoris in the far north, but the lander's laser rangefinder was too slow and it hit the ground.
sites.fun_fact: The crash left a dark smudge on the Moon that NASA's orbiter photographed six days later.
sites.label: Fact
